stops.title: The oldest Homo sapiens: Jebel Irhoud
stops.dateNote: Flint tools heated in fires date the fossils to 315,000 years ago, give or take 34,000; a tooth gave 286,000, give or take 32,000. The timeline starts at 300,000 years ago, so the stop sits there.
stops.blurb: At Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, excavators found skulls, jaws and teeth of early humans lying with stone tools. Flint tools that had been heated in fires date them to about 315,000 years ago. Their faces and teeth look much like ours, but the braincase keeps an older, more primitive shape. They are the oldest fossils yet assigned to our species, Homo sapiens.

stops.title: New tools, and stone from far away
stops.dateNote: Argon and uranium-series dates put the earliest Middle Stone Age layers at Olorgesailie between about 320,000 and 295,000 years ago. The timeline starts at 300,000 years ago, so the stop sits there.
stops.blurb: In the Olorgesailie basin of southern Kenya, people made large hand axes for hundreds of thousands of years. By about 320,000 years ago they were making smaller, carefully shaped points instead, the start of what archaeologists call the Middle Stone Age. The basin has no obsidian, a volcanic glass, yet tools there were made from obsidian found 25 to about 90 kilometres away.

stops.title: Not the only humans
stops.dateNote: Each species has its own dates. The map shows the world about 275,000 years ago.
stops.blurb: Homo sapiens shared the world with other kinds of human. Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia, and Denisovans further east. In South Africa the small-brained Homo naledi lived between about 335,000 and 236,000 years ago, and the Broken Hill skull from Zambia, of a different lineage, is about 299,000 years old. On Java, Homo erectus lasted until about 110,000 years ago.

stops.title: Many cradles across Africa
stops.dateNote: Florisbad is dated to about 260,000 years ago. For Omo I, 233,000 years ago is a minimum age: the fossil lies below a volcanic ash of that age.
stops.blurb: Jebel Irhoud lies in the far northwest of Africa, but other early fossils with some features like ours come from the south and east. A skull from Florisbad in South Africa is about 260,000 years old, and the Omo I skull from Ethiopia is at least 233,000. Many researchers now think our species took shape across the continent, among groups that split, met and mixed over a long time.
stops.debate: Scerri and colleagues argue that our species formed among many linked populations across Africa, against the older view of one population in one region; the few fossils cannot yet settle it.

stops.title: Early ventures out of Africa
stops.dateNote: Misliya is dated to 194,000 to 177,000 years ago, a date that is disputed. Skhul and Qafzeh fall roughly between 130,000 and 90,000 years ago.
stops.blurb: People of our species left Africa long before the migration that gave rise to most people outside Africa today. A jaw with teeth from Misliya Cave in Israel has been dated to between 194,000 and 177,000 years ago. Burials at Skhul and Qafzeh, also in Israel, date to roughly 130,000 to 90,000 years ago. Ancient DNA suggests an early African group even mixed with Neanderthals.
stops.debate: Sharp and Paces argue that the uranium-series data give the Misliya jaw a minimum age of only about 60,000 to 70,000 years; the excavators defend the older date.

stops.title: Living by the sea
stops.dateNote: The shellfish layers at Pinnacle Point are dated to about 164,000 years ago, give or take 12,000.
stops.blurb: In a cave at Pinnacle Point on the south coast of South Africa, people were eating shellfish by about 164,000 years ago, the oldest known use of food from the sea. Much of Africa was then cold and dry. The same layers hold red pigment that had been worked, tiny blade tools, and stone that had been heated so it would flake more easily.

stops.title: Beads, ochre and the first patterns
stops.dateNote: The Bizmoune beads are at least 142,000 years old; the Blombos finds range from about 100,000 to 73,000 years ago.
stops.blurb: Some of the oldest known ornaments are small sea-snail shells, pierced and worn as beads. At Bizmoune Cave in Morocco they are at least 142,000 years old. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, people mixed a red ochre paste in abalone shells 100,000 years ago, engraved lines on lumps of ochre, and about 73,000 years ago drew crossed lines on a stone flake.

stops.title: When did language begin?
stops.dateNote: No date can be fixed. 135,000 years ago is one recent estimate of the latest time by which the capacity for language existed; others put it far earlier.
stops.blurb: Speech leaves no fossils, so nobody knows when language began. Every human population today has full language, so the capacity probably existed before the oldest splits between living populations, which genetic studies place about 135,000 years ago. Some researchers argue that Neanderthals could speak too, which would push language back half a million years or more. The evidence does not yet decide it.
stops.debate: Miyagawa and colleagues argue the capacity for language existed by 135,000 years ago at the latest; Dediu and Levinson argue that it goes back to the common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans, more than half a million years ago.

stops.title: When the Sahara turned green
stops.dateNote: Green Sahara periods came and went many times. This stop shows the one around 125,000 years ago, in the last warm interglacial.
stops.blurb: The Sahara has not always been a desert. Changes in Earth's orbit strengthen the African monsoon from time to time, and in the last eight million years the Sahara turned green more than 230 times. Each green phase lasted several thousand years. About 125,000 years ago, green corridors crossed it, possible paths north for animals and perhaps for people.

stops.title: Fire and cooking
stops.dateNote: Burning in Wonderwerk Cave is about a million years old; the cooked starchy plants at Klasies River are about 120,000 years old.
stops.blurb: Our species inherited fire from older humans. Burnt bone and plant ash show fires inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa about a million years ago, and pyrite found with burnt flint at Barnham in England suggests fire was being made there 400,000 years ago. Early Homo sapiens heated stone to make it flake better, and cooked starchy plants in hearths at Klasies River 120,000 years ago.

links.label: Control of fire by early humans

stops.title: The oldest known burial in Africa
stops.dateNote: The burial is dated to 78,300 years ago, give or take 4,100.
stops.blurb: About 78,000 years ago, in the cave of Panga ya Saidi near the coast of Kenya, a child of two and a half to three years was laid in a dug pit with legs drawn up, and covered with earth. The bones were still joined, so the body decayed where it was placed. It is the oldest known human burial in Africa, though burials at Skhul and Qafzeh are older.
stops.debate: Berger and colleagues argue that Homo naledi buried its dead in Rising Star Cave more than 236,000 years ago; Martinón-Torres and colleagues reply that natural causes have not been ruled out.

stops.title: The Toba eruption
stops.dateNote: The eruption is dated to about 74,000 years ago.
stops.blurb: About 74,000 years ago the Toba volcano on Sumatra erupted, the most explosive eruption of the last 2.6 million years. Its ash fell across the Indian Ocean and as far as South Africa. One theory held that the cold that followed nearly wiped out our species. Yet at sites in India and South Africa, people went on living and making tools above and below the ash.
stops.debate: Ambrose proposed that Toba's volcanic winter caused a human population bottleneck; ash in Lake Malawi shows no major cooling in East Africa, and sites in India and South Africa show people living through it.

p: For much of the twentieth century, the search for the first members of our species focused on East Africa. The oldest fossils that looked fully modern came from there, and the story was told as if Homo sapiens had appeared in one place at one time. That picture has changed. The oldest fossils now assigned to our species come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 315,000 years ago. A skull from Florisbad in South Africa is about 260,000 years old. In Ethiopia, the Omo I skull, once dated to about 197,000 years ago, is now known to be at least 233,000 years old. Early fossils with some modern features are spread from one end of Africa to the other.

The dates come from several methods. At Jebel Irhoud, flint tools burnt in ancient fires were dated by thermoluminescence, which measures the energy stored in crystals since they were last heated. At Omo, the fossil lies beneath a layer of volcanic ash. In 2022 a team matched that ash to a large eruption of the Shala volcano in the Ethiopian Rift and dated the eruption, which gave a minimum age for the skull. The fossils do not all look alike. The Jebel Irhoud people had faces like ours but long, low braincases. A rounder braincase seems to have come later. Genetic studies of living Africans also show divisions between populations that go back a very long way.

In 2018 Eleanor Scerri and colleagues argued that our species did not evolve in a single population or region. They pointed to the spread of the fossils, to regional styles of stone tools that lasted a long time, and to climate records showing that habitable areas kept splitting and joining. In this view, groups lived apart for long periods and then met and mixed again, and modern humans are the result of that whole network. A 2021 review of the genetic evidence reached a similar conclusion: no single point in time can yet be identified when our ancestors were confined to one small birthplace. Other researchers still give more weight to a single region. There are very few fossils, so every view rests on thin evidence.

The idea of a single cradle is simple and easy to draw on a map, but the evidence fits a messier story. If our species formed across a whole continent, then the deep roots of every person alive today lie in many parts of Africa at once. It also means that the deep splits between populations in Africa today belong to the same long history.

Most people whose ancestry lies outside Africa descend from a migration that began about 60,000 to 50,000 years ago, told in chapter 2. But it was not the first time people of our species left Africa. Fossils from southwest Asia, and perhaps southern Europe, show earlier ventures. A jaw with teeth found in Misliya Cave in Israel has been dated to between 194,000 and 177,000 years ago. A damaged, incomplete skull from Apidima Cave in southern Greece, dated to more than 210,000 years ago, mixes modern and primitive features. Later, between roughly 130,000 and 90,000 years ago, people buried their dead in the caves of Skhul and Qafzeh in Israel.

The shape of the Misliya jaw and teeth matches Homo sapiens, and the jaw was found with stone tools made by the Levallois method, a way of preparing a stone core so that flakes of a planned shape can be struck from it. At Skhul, uranium-series and electron spin resonance dates on bones and teeth agree with dates on burnt flint, and place the burials between about 135,000 and 100,000 years ago. Neanderthals lived in the same region around the same time, at nearby Tabun. DNA gives another clue. A Neanderthal thigh bone from Germany carries a type of mitochondrial DNA that suggests Neanderthals received genes from an African population some time between about 270,000 and 100,000 years ago.

Each early find has its doubters. Geologists Warren Sharp and James Paces argued that the uranium-series results for the Misliya jaw had been misread and gave only a minimum age of about 60,000 to 70,000 years. The excavators replied and kept their date. The claim for Apidima rests on one incomplete skull. A broader question is what became of these groups. The later migration accounts for nearly all the ancestry of people outside Africa today, so the early groups seem to have died out or been absorbed. No DNA has been recovered from the fossils themselves to test this.

These finds show that leaving Africa was not a single event. Groups of our species moved into southwest Asia and perhaps Europe more than once, and met Neanderthals there. Most of these ventures did not last. They help explain why the later, successful migration found a world where the two kinds of human had already met, and why Neanderthal genomes carry traces of early Africans.

Long before cave paintings in Europe, people in Africa were making objects that seem to have had no practical use. They pierced small sea-snail shells and wore them as beads. They ground red ochre, an iron-rich earth, into powder and paste. They scratched patterns into lumps of ochre and onto stone. The oldest known beads come from Bizmoune Cave near Essaouira in Morocco, in layers at least 142,000 years old. Similar beads, made from the same kind of shell, appear at Taforalt in eastern Morocco about 82,000 years ago. At Blombos Cave, on the south coast of South Africa, the finds span from about 100,000 to 73,000 years ago.

The beads are shells of tiny sea snails, carried to the caves from the shore. Microscope studies of the Blombos shells show that the holes were punched through the shell wall, not made by predators or wear on the beach, and that wear around the holes came from being strung and worn. Several groups of beads were found together, each matching in colour and wear, as if from the same necklace or garment. Some Taforalt shells were covered in red ochre. At Blombos, excavators also found two abalone shells that had held a liquid mixture rich in ochre, lying with bone, charcoal, grindstones and hammerstones used to make it. Thirteen pieces of ochre from the same cave carry deliberately engraved lines, and a flake of stone from the 73,000-year-old layer has crossed lines drawn on it with an ochre crayon.

Archaeologists often treat beads and patterns as signs of symbolic thinking, the ability to let one thing stand for another, such as a person's group or status. The researchers at Bizmoune suggest the beads were signals of identity. But what the objects meant to the people who made them cannot be recovered, and the use of the Blombos ochre paste is unknown: decoration and protecting the skin are both possible. There is also an older argument about timing. Some researchers once linked "modern" behaviour to a burst of change after about 50,000 years ago, when such objects become common in Europe and elsewhere. The African finds show that beads and engraving appeared much earlier.

Beads are among the earliest objects made to be seen by others. Wearing them only makes sense among people who notice and read such signals. The finds from Morocco and South Africa, thousands of kilometres apart, show that habits like these were part of life for Homo sapiens in Africa tens of thousands of years before similar objects appear in Europe.

At some point, humans began to speak in full language: words combined by rules into an unlimited number of sentences. Every human group living today has language of this kind, and none has a simpler or more primitive form. That much is certain. When language began, and whether other kinds of human had it too, is not known. Speech leaves no direct trace, and writing appeared only about 5,000 years ago.

All the evidence is indirect. One line comes from genetics. If all living populations share the capacity for language, it probably existed before those populations first split apart. In 2025 Shigeru Miyagawa and colleagues reviewed genome studies that place the earliest split within Homo sapiens at about 135,000 years ago, and argued that the capacity must have been present by then at the latest. A second line compares Neanderthals with us: Dediu and Levinson gathered evidence from their skeletons, genes and archaeology suggesting that they shared something like modern speech. A third comes from archaeology: objects such as beads and engraved patterns suggest people who used symbols, and many researchers think symbols and language are closely tied. Beads from Bizmoune Cave in Morocco show such objects by at least 142,000 years ago.

Almost everything. The usual view in the late twentieth century placed the origin of language between about 100,000 and 50,000 years ago, sometimes as the result of a single sudden genetic change. In 2013 Dan Dediu and Stephen Levinson argued instead that language is much older, going back at least to the common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans, about half a million years ago, and that it evolved gradually. Miyagawa's group sets a latest date rather than an earliest one, and suggests that language may have helped bring about the wider spread of symbolic behaviour around 100,000 years ago. These positions rest on different kinds of evidence, and none can be tested directly.

Language lets people share plans, teach skills, keep track of relatives and allies, and pass on knowledge across generations. Much of what makes human societies possible depends on it. Knowing when it appeared would help explain when and why our ancestors began to behave in ways we recognise. For now, the honest answer is that the capacity was there by around 135,000 years ago, and may be far older.
